parameters.content:
### DataHub Enrichment (via MCP)

Reads DataHub through the open-source **mcp-server-datahub**
(no direct GraphQL). Calls the FastAPI bridge at
`host.docker.internal:8010/mcp/enrich`, which invokes:

- `search` — resolve table name to dataset URN
- `get_entities` — tags, glossary terms, owners
- `get_lineage` — downstream blast radius (destructive actions only)

**Outputs `datahub_context`:**
| field | meaning |
|---|---|
| resolved | metadata found in catalogue |
| dataset / platform | table name, snowflake or postgres |
| action | delete / export / deploy / read |
| classification | PII, Confidential, Internal, Public |
| tags | GDPR, PCI, Financial, etc. |
| owner | steward from DataHub ownership |
| downstream_count | tables that break if this is deleted |
| mcp_tools_used | audit trail of MCP calls |

LLM extracts facts. Deterministic code decides.

### Decision Engine
**This is where the answer is decided.**
Every step before this one just collects information.
This step is the only one that says yes or no.
**No AI is used here, on purpose.**
An AI can be tricked by clever wording. So the AI is only
allowed to look and report what it sees. It is never allowed
to choose. The choosing is done by simple rules that always
work the same way. Ask the same question twice, get the same
answer twice. And you can always show someone exactly which
rule made the choice.

**How it chooses:**
Four helpers check the request at the same time. Each one
looks for a different kind of problem. If even one helper
says "this is not okay", the answer is no. Three happy
helpers cannot cancel out one worried helper. The most
careful one always wins.

**What it gives back:**

| name | what it means |
|---|---|
| decision | `approve` = go ahead. `deny` = stop. `human_review` = wait, ask a person first |
| risk_score | a number from 0 to 100. Bigger number = more dangerous |
| risk_tier | the same thing in words: low, medium or high |
| checks | which helpers were happy. `false` means that helper was worried |
| datahub_context | the facts about the table, kept here so we can always look back and see the reason for the answer |

**Why the facts matter:**
"Delete this table" sounds the same every single time.
But deleting a table of people's names and addresses is very
different from deleting a table of product prices. And if
other tables are built on top of it, they all break too.
The only way to know the difference is to look it up first.
That is what DataHub is for.

## I'm a note 
### Policy Retrieval

**This step goes and finds the relevant rules.**

The gateway does not keep the law in its head. It keeps a
searchable library of regulation — EU AI Act, GDPR, UK
guidance — chopped into small passages.

**It searches two different ways at once.**

The first way looks for *meaning*. Every passage is turned
into numbers that capture what it is about. So a request
about "removing customer records" can find a rule about
"erasure of personal data", even though they share no words.

The second way looks for *exact words*. This matters because
legal text is full of precise labels like "Article 5(1)(c)".
Meaning-based search blurs those together — Article 5 and
Article 6 look almost identical to it. Word matching does not
blur. It finds the exact one.

**Then it combines the two lists.**
A passage that both ways agree on rises to the top. A passage
only one way found still gets a place, because it might be the
thing the other way missed.

**What comes back:** a handful of real regulation passages,
each with its source and article number, and a note saying
which method found it. The next step reasons using these
instead of relying on whatever the AI happens to remember.

### Audit Log

**This is the permanent record.**

Every time the gateway makes a decision, one line is written
to a database. Nothing is ever changed or deleted afterwards.

Why bother? Because if someone asks six months from now
"why did the AI refuse to do that?" — the answer has to
still exist. A decision nobody can explain later is not
really governance.

**What each line saves:**

| column | in plain words |
|---|---|
| id | a counter, so every line has its own number |
| decided_at | the exact date and time this was decided |
| agent_id | which AI was asking |
| user_id | who the AI was working for |
| action | what it wanted to do — delete, export, deploy |
| target | which table it wanted to do it to |
| classification | how sensitive that table is (PII, Public...) |
| downstream_count | how many other tables would break |
| decision | what we said: approve, deny, or ask a person |
| risk_score | how dangerous it was, 0 to 100 |
| reasons | the full list of why — every rule that objected |

**The important columns are the last four.** The others say
*what happened*. Those say *why* — and that is the part an
auditor actually asks for.
